topic: Constitutional Law and Polity: Union and State Executive and Legislature
description: This module delves into the structure and functioning of the government at both the central (Union) and state levels. It outlines the parliamentary system of government, distinguishing between the nominal and real executives, and explains the composition and powers of the legislative bodies (Parliament and State Legislatures).

the_executive_nominal_vs_real.concept: The Executive: Nominal and Real Heads
key_points: Union Executive: Consists of the President, Vice-President, Prime Minister, Council of Ministers, and Attorney General. The President is the nominal head (De Jure), while the Prime Minister is the real executive head (De Facto).

State Executive: Consists of the Governor, Chief Minister, Council of Ministers, and Advocate General. Similar to the center, the Governor is the nominal head acting on the advice of the Chief Minister (the real head).
Binding Advice: Under Article 74, the President shall act in accordance with the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the PM (made binding by the 42nd and 44th Amendments).

the_legislature_structure.concept: The Legislature: Parliament and State Legislatures
key_points: Union Parliament (Article 79): The Parliament of India consists of three parts: The President, the Council of States (Rajya Sabha - Upper House), and the House of the People (Lok Sabha - Lower House). The President is an integral part of Parliament, though not a member of either house.
State Legislature: Consists of the Governor and the Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha). Some states have a bicameral legislature, which also includes a Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad).
Law-Making Process: A bill must be passed by both houses (where applicable) and receive the assent of the President/Governor to become an Act.
Core Principle: The bedrock of the parliamentary system. Article 75(3) states that the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Lower House).
Meaning: The ministers swim and sink together. If a motion of no-confidence is passed by the Lok Sabha, the entire Council of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, must resign.
State Level: Similarly, Article 164(2) makes the state Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the State Legislative Assembly.

questions.question: According to Article 79 of the Indian Constitution, the Parliament of the Union consists of:

options.A: The Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha only
options.B: The Prime Minister, the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha
options.C: The President, the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha
options.D: The President, the Vice-President, and the Lok Sabha

questions.explanation: Article 79 explicitly states that there shall be a Parliament for the Union which shall consist of the President and two Houses to be known respectively as the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) and the House of the People (Lok Sabha).

questions.question: During a parliamentary session, a major policy introduced by the Minister of Finance fails to garner support, and the opposition successfully passes a 'No-Confidence Motion' in the Lok Sabha. What is the immediate constitutional consequence?

options.A: Only the Minister of Finance is forced to resign.
options.B: The President assumes dictatorial powers and dissolves the Constitution.
options.C: The entire Council of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, must resign.
options.D: The bill is sent to the Rajya Sabha for a final decision.

questions.explanation: Due to the principle of 'Collective Responsibility' enshrined in Article 75(3), a government only remains in power as long as it enjoys the majority support of the Lok Sabha. A successful no-confidence motion means the entire government (Council of Ministers) falls and must resign.

questions.question: Why is the President of India bound by the advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74), unlike the President of the United States who enjoys absolute executive authority?

options.A: Because the Indian Constitution establishes a Parliamentary form of government where the real executive power vests in the Council of Ministers responsible to the legislature, making the President a nominal head.
options.B: Because the President of India is not a citizen by birth and thus has limited powers.
options.C: Because the Supreme Court of India drafts the policies, and the President only signs them.
options.D: Because the Indian Constitution is completely unitary and does not recognize executive powers.

questions.explanation: India adopted the British model of a Parliamentary democracy rather than the American Presidential system. In a parliamentary system, to prevent authoritarianism and ensure accountability to the people (via the legislature), the real executive power lies with the elected Prime Minister and their cabinet, rendering the President a nominal or constitutional head.
